661.quote_or_event: “The mind is that unruly, dreadful, bad horse; I govern it by the discipline of the Law”
661.explanation: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, Gautama explains that the horse which never runs off with him is his own mind, held in check by the discipline of the Law.
661.tie_back: Like the kural, Jainism locates real strength in the steadied mind rather than in any outward power, since everything else follows from whether the mind is mastered.
661.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.58 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
661._accuracy_note: Close on the core claim that firmness lies in the mind; the Jain goal is spiritual self-mastery rather than success in worldly undertakings.

662.quote_or_event: “twenty-two troubles which a monk must learn and know, bear and conquer, in order not to be vanquished by them when he lives the life of a wandering mendicant.”
662.explanation: Mahavira's teaching on the parisahas (troubles) asks the monk to know the hardships in advance and to bear them without being overcome when they arrive.
662.tie_back: This mirrors the kural's two rules of firmness: prepare against harm before it comes, and do not give way once it has come.
662.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra, Lecture 2, prose introduction (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
662._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel (foreknowledge plus endurance), though the Jain text concerns ascetic hardships rather than avoiding harm to a worldly enterprise.

663.quote_or_event: “A monk should avoid untruth, nor should he speak positively (about future things, his plans, &c.)”
663.explanation: Among the rules of discipline, a monk is told not to make confident declarations about future things or his own plans, as part of guarding his speech from untruth.
663.tie_back: The kural's advice that a task should become known only when it is done finds a partial echo in this Jain restraint on announcing one's plans before they are fulfilled.
663.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
663._accuracy_note: Partial match only: the Jain motive is truthfulness and restraint of speech (the parenthetical gloss is Jacobi's), not strategic secrecy to keep a project from being undone.

664.quote_or_event: “Acknowledging the truth about bondage and liberation, but talking only, not acting (in accordance with these tenets), they seek comfort for themselves in mighty words. Clever talking will not work salvation”
664.explanation: Mahavira criticises those who can expound the doctrine of bondage and liberation but do not live by it, trusting in words instead of deeds.
664.tie_back: The kural's point that saying how a thing should be done is easy while doing it as said is hard is exactly the gap this verse condemns.
664.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.9-10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
664._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the contrast of word and deed; the Jain context is spiritual practice rather than carrying out a minister's counsel.

665.quote_or_event: “An intelligent man who has learned (the sacred texts) takes his duties upon himself, and he becomes renowned in the world; as the earth is the dwelling of all beings, so he will be a dwelling of all duties.”
665.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's lecture on discipline says the pupil who reliably shoulders his duties becomes renowned, and goes on to say he will be honoured by gods, Gandharvas and men.
665.tie_back: Just as the kural says the firmness of eminent men reaches the king and wins general esteem, the Jain text makes steadfast discharge of duty the source of a person's renown.
665.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.45 (cf. 1.48) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
665._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on renown earned by dependable action, but the Jain setting is a monastic pupil, not a servant whose firmness reaches a king.

666.quote_or_event: “But he who has renounced pleasure, will not miss his aim”
666.explanation: In the parable of the ram, the Uttaradhyayana contrasts the one who, though taught the right way, goes astray again and again with the one who has renounced pleasure and therefore does not miss his aim.
666.tie_back: Like the kural's promise that the firm will attain what they planned, this verse makes steadiness of purpose the condition for reaching one's goal.
666.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.25-26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
666._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit on firmness securing the aim; the Jain aim is spiritual (the true end of the soul, per Jacobi's gloss on 7.25) rather than worldly plans.

667.quote_or_event: “Who is that dandy coming there? he is swarthy, dreadful, with a turned-up nose, miserably clad, a very devil of a dirty man”
667.explanation: The Brahmin priests mock the outcaste monk Harikesa for his looks and poverty, until his spiritual power is revealed and they cry that the value of penance has become visible and birth appears of no value.
667.tie_back: The story enacts the kural's warning not to despise anyone for small size or plain appearance, for the scorned figure proves to be the one on whom everything turns.
667.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.6 and 12.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
667._accuracy_note: Strong narrative fit for not judging by appearance; the Jain point is about birth and ascetic merit rather than a small but vital helper like the linchpin.

668.quote_or_event: “Now you have entered on the path from which the thorns have been cleared, the great path; walk in the right path; Gautama, &c. Do not get into an uneven road like a weak burden-bearer; for you will repent of it afterwards”
668.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama that, the path now being clear, he should walk it steadily and not stray onto an uneven road, ending each verse with the refrain to be careful all the while.
668.tie_back: The kural's counsel to carry out without wavering a course settled with a clear mind matches this call to keep to a path already seen clearly.
668.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.32-33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
668._accuracy_note: Fits the no-wavering element well; the no-delay element is only implied by the lecture's refrain against carelessness (pramada).

669.quote_or_event: “If any misfortune happens and he suffers pain, he should cheerfully steady his mind, and bear the ills that attack him.”
669.explanation: In the lecture on troubles the monk is told to meet misfortune and pain with a steadied, cheerful mind, bearing it for the sake of the welfare of his soul.
669.tie_back: This parallels the kural's call to press on courageously through great hardship toward the work that brings joy at the end.
669.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
669._accuracy_note: Strong fit on enduring hardship with a steady mind; the 'joy at the end' in Jainism is liberation, and the verse itself does not name the end reward.

670.quote_or_event: “Just as bad bullocks are when put before a car, so are bad pupils when yoked, as it were, to the car of the Law; they break down through want of zeal.”
670.explanation: The teacher Garga, wearied by pupils who balk and wander like unruly bullocks, finally leaves those lazy donkeys and goes his own way in austerity.
670.tie_back: As the kural says the world does not value those who do not value firmness in action, the Jain parable shows the zealless being given up as useless by their own teacher.
670.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 27.8 (cf. 27.16) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
670._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on the worthlessness of those without steadiness; the Jain text is about monastic pupils and their teacher rather than the world's esteem.
